directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; ashy hydrangea is closely related to smooth hydrangea and shares its tolerance for shade and adaptable garden soil. Hydrangea cinerea is a southeastern native shrub closely related to and sometimes treated as a variety of smooth hydrangea, distinguished by the fine, ashy-gray down covering the undersides of its leaves, with flattened clusters of small white fertile flowers ringed by a few showier sterile florets in early summer. Its shade tolerance and adaptability to typical garden soil make it a reliable native alternative to Hydrangea arborescens cultivars for a woodland border or native shrub planting, blooming reliably on new wood even after a hard late-winter pruning. Cut stems back by a third to a half in late winter to encourage strong new growth and the best flowering the following summer.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pride of Rochester grows considerably taller and more upright than dwarf deutzia cultivars and needs room to reach its full arching, vase-shaped mature size.

directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pride of Rochester grows considerably taller and more upright than dwarf deutzia cultivars and needs room to reach its full arching, vase-shaped mature size. This heirloom nineteenth-century deutzia cultivar produces an abundance of double, pale pink-tinged white flowers packed densely along arching branches in late spring, one of the showiest bloom displays among old-fashioned flowering shrubs, followed by peeling, cinnamon-colored bark that adds winter interest. Its large size and old-fashioned charm make it a good choice for the back of a shrub border, an informal flowering hedge, or a specimen where its fountain-like form and heavy spring bloom can be fully appreciated. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes to the ground right after flowering each year to keep the shrub vigorous and well-shaped over time.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Mexican anise tree has the most vividly colored flowers of the cultivated Illicium species and benefits from a sheltered site at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.

directions: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Mexican anise tree has the most vividly colored flowers of the cultivated Illicium species and benefits from a sheltered site at the cooler edge of its hardiness range. Illicium mexicanum is a Mexican relative of the southeastern native Florida anise, grown for its glossy, aromatic, evergreen leaves and striking, star-shaped, deep wine-red to burgundy flowers produced over an unusually long season from spring into summer, showier and more prolonged in bloom than most anise tree species. Its rich flower color and dense evergreen habit make it a distinctive specimen or informal screen for a shaded border, tolerating deep shade better than most flowering evergreens. Give it consistently moist, acidic soil similar to camellia and azalea, and protect from hard freezes at the colder edge of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; 'Rubella' is a male-flowering selection grown for its ornamental winter buds and fragrant spring flowers rather than for berries, since it does not set fruit.

directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; 'Rubella' is a male-flowering selection grown for its ornamental winter buds and fragrant spring flowers rather than for berries, since it does not set fruit. This compact, mounding, evergreen skimmia selection is prized for its conspicuous red flower buds that form in fall and persist ornamentally through winter, opening in early spring into fragrant clusters of small white flowers with red-tinged anthers that scent the garden. Because 'Rubella' is a male clone it produces no berries itself, but it is an excellent pollinator for female skimmia cultivars grown nearby for their showy red winter fruit, and its dense, glossy foliage and winter buds provide year-round interest on their own. It thrives in deep shade where few flowering evergreens perform well, making it a valuable choice for a shaded foundation planting or woodland garden.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Spider's Web' is less vigorous and more cold-sensitive than plain green fatsia, so give it a sheltered site or grow it in a container that can be moved for winter protection.

directions: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Spider's Web' is less vigorous and more cold-sensitive than plain green fatsia, so give it a sheltered site or grow it in a container that can be moved for winter protection. This striking fatsia selection carries the same bold, glossy, deeply lobed, tropical-textured leaves as the species but heavily speckled and mottled with white, giving each leaf a frosted, web-like appearance that brightens a deeply shaded corner. Rounded clusters of small white flowers appear in fall on mature plants, followed by black berries, though the plant is grown almost entirely for its dramatic variegated foliage rather than its modest bloom. Because variegated growth is less vigorous than solid green fatsia, prune out any reverted all-green shoots promptly to keep the plant's variegation strong, and protect from hard freezes and drying winter wind at the colder edge of its range.
